doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Composers as improvisers; harmony in Beethoven and Mozart
summary: Classical giants improvised; Hanna hears jazz harmonies such as flatted ninths in Beethoven and Mozart, and notes composers' fear of patrons.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Isn’t it curious that a lot of classical musicians are enamored sometimes of what a jazz player can do. At the same time a jazz musician looks at what they do.

Well you know it always seemed to me that the guys who really are the giants are the composers who recognize how important it is to improvise. Rachmaninoff was a great improviser. Anton Rubenstein was a great improviser. Bussoni, Tosic, they were great improvisers. They could sit down and improvise on a Bach fugue. And anybody who plays the fugues, they know what I’m talking about. They know how difficult it is to do that. But they were also people who analyzed constantly. They were never people who just played notes. And that’s the unfortunate thing that sometimes young students don’t get the understanding that you have to know the form, the shape, the harmonies and you have to go beyond triad harmonies you see. Some classical people never go beyond triadic harmonies. When they do begin to understand that there’s more than just passing tones and upper neighbors, well then they start to make really good music.
So when you play Mozart or Beethoven, you’re most likely recognizing the harmonies as they go by.

Yes. All the variations and nuances that are put in. Like for instance in the Appassionata, the last movement, Beethoven is using the diminished chord over a pedal point you know. That flatted ninth that we call today in jazz, that, Beethoven may not have called it a flatted ninth, but he certainly heard it the same way we are hearing it now. And there are certain things that happen in Mozart. Mozart also was a guy who loved to make flatted ninths, but he would move them right away. See they were afraid of society, more afraid of society than we are today. They were afraid of overlords, people who would come and stop them from playing music if they did music a certain way. Look at Haydn, Franz Joseph Haydn, the “Farewell Symphony.” There’s an example of how afraid they were.
Right. He couldn’t come out and say what he wanted to.
